patient.key: 35M, 3-week Caribbean cruise with social boozing. Symptoms began 7 days ago. Emergency stop on island: treated with anti-emetic only, discharged. Flight home: skin turned yellow. Wife rushes him to ED — vomiting flooding the car. Aspiration event during transport. AST 3117, ALT 2362, Tbili 23.7. Hepatitis A IgM positive. Fetor hepaticus.

history.hpi: 35M to ED with sharp 7/10 RUQ pain worsening with movement, improving with rest. SOB, pain with deep breaths. 3-week Caribbean cruise with social boozing (1-2 drinks/day, more than usual). Symptoms began 7 days ago: fatigue, subjective fever, chills, poor appetite, nausea, intractable vomiting, intermittent chest pain. Emergency stop made on a Caribbean island on his behalf — treated with anti-emetic and discharged with minimal symptomatic improvement. On flight home after cruise: skin turned yellow-tinged, developed severe pruritis. Wife reports 'putrid breath' since illness. Wife rushes him to ED upon return — vomiting flooding the car during transport. Aspiration event during the car ride to the hospital.
history.social: Married, 2 children (7 & 5). Children stayed with grandparents during cruise. No smoking. Social drinker. No illicit substances.
history.family: Father 68, healthy. Mother has hypertension, controlled.
history.ros: General: see HPI. Skin: negative. HEENT: negative. Cardiorespiratory: negative. GI: see HPI. GU: negative. Neuropsychiatric: negative.

physicalExam.general: Well-developed, well-nourished, diaphoretic, ill-appearing male in mild to moderate distress.
physicalExam.skin: Decreased skin turgor. Jaundiced skin. No nodules or lesions.
physicalExam.heent: Normocephalic. Foul-smelling breath and sputum (fetor hepaticus). Mucous membranes moist. Neck supple.
physicalExam.chestLungs: Shallow breathing. Bilateral wheezing on auscultation. Hypo-resonance with percussion in right lower lobe. Diaphragm and chest move equally.
physicalExam.heart: S1/S2 normal. No murmurs, rubs, gallops. No JVD. BP equal in both arms.
physicalExam.abdomen: Tender to palpation in RUQ. Hepatomegaly. Bowel sounds normal. No hernias.
physicalExam.rectal: Sphincter tone normal. No masses. Stool brown, no occult blood. Prostate normal.
physicalExam.extremities: No edema, cyanosis, clubbing. Peripheral pulses normal. Full ROM.
physicalExam.neuro: Mental status normal. Cranial nerves, motor, sensory normal. DTRs normal.

labs.hepatitisPanel: Hepatitis A IgM positive. HBsAg negative. HCV antibody negative.

ordersPlaced: Physical Exam: General Appearance, Skin, Lymph Node, HEENT, Chest/Lungs, Heart, Abdomen, Genital, Rectal, Extremities/Spine, Neuro/Psych

missed.why: AST 3117, ALT 2362 in a young person. Acetaminophen overdose is the #1 cause of acute liver failure in the US. Must rule out before calling it viral. If positive, start NAC immediately.
Patient says he can't breathe. So simple, so fundamental — free, non-invasive, and it tells you how bad the hypoxia is.

missed.order: Antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia (levofloxacin, ceftriaxone + azithromycin, or ampicillin-sulbactam)
missed.why: CXR confirmed aspiration pneumonia. ATS/IDSA guidelines: treat like community-acquired pneumonia. Anaerobic coverage NOT needed unless empyema or abscess. Cefepime + vancomycin is wrong — that's HAP/VAP with MRSA/Pseudomonas risk, not community aspiration.
Hepatitis A is fecal-oral transmission. Contact precautions protect staff and other patients. Family needs post-exposure prophylaxis (HAV vaccine or immunoglobulin).

missed.order: Transfer to Inpatient Unit or ICU
missed.why: Patient with AST >3000, Tbili 23.7, hyponatremic, hypokalemic, aspiration pneumonia, and intractable vomiting needs inpatient monitoring. LFTs must trend downward before discharge. Location error cost 50%.
Tbili 23.7 with impaired synthetic function (albumin 2.5). INR likely elevated. Vitamin K corrects coagulopathy from vitamin K malabsorption in cholestasis.
Assess synthetic liver function. Prolonged PT/INR indicates impaired hepatic synthesis of clotting factors — prognostic in acute liver failure.
Intractable vomiting. NPO until vomiting controlled. Avoid hepatotoxic medications.

correctlyAvoided: Acetaminophen therapy (would be hepatotoxic given AST >3000, ALT >2000)
Meperidine (normeperidine accumulation in hepatic impairment → neurotoxicity, seizures)

errors.detail: Intubation, endotracheal + Mechanical ventilation at Day 1 18:47. Considered inappropriate/invasive for this case (0% on appropriate orders). Patient had aspiration pneumonia but did not meet criteria for intubation — oxygen alone would suffice.
Stayed in Emergency Department. At simulated time 0 Days 08 Hours 00 Minutes, correct location was ICU or Inpatient Unit. Patient needed monitoring of LFTs downward trajectory.
1 negative patient update prior to correct treatment (0% on timing)
Octreotide — indicated for variceal bleeding and hepatorenal syndrome. This patient has hepatitis A with no portal hypertension, no varices. Not indicated.

pathophysiology.hepatitisA: HAV is an RNA picornavirus transmitted via fecal-oral route. Common in areas with poor sanitation and on cruise ships (contaminated food/water). Incubation 15-50 days (avg 28). Causes acute hepatocellular injury → transaminases rise (ALT > AST in viral hepatitis usually, but both can be >1000). Jaundice from impaired bilirubin conjugation and excretion. Self-limited illness — fulminant hepatic failure is rare (<1%) but more common with underlying liver disease (especially HCV).
pathophysiology.aspirationPneumonia: Intractable vomiting → aspiration of gastric contents → chemical pneumonitis → secondary bacterial infection. RLL most common (dependent position). Foul-smelling breath = fetor hepaticus from portosystemic shunting of sulfur compounds, NOT from the pneumonia itself.
pathophysiology.fetorHepaticus: Dimethyl sulfide and other volatile sulfur compounds bypass hepatic metabolism via portosystemic shunting → exhaled in breath → sweet, musty, 'dead mouse' odor. Sign of significant hepatocellular dysfunction. Not necessarily portal hypertension — acute hepatitis can cause transient intrahepatic shunting.

teachingPoints: Acetaminophen toxicity is the #1 cause of acute liver failure. Always check an acetaminophen level with AST/ALT >1000, even if the patient 'didn't take any.' History is unreliable.
Aspiration pneumonia in ATS/IDSA guidelines = treat like community-acquired pneumonia. Anaerobic coverage only if empyema or abscess.
Fetor hepaticus = portosystemic shunting of sulfur compounds. Smell before you see it on labs.
Octreotide is for variceal bleeding (portal hypertension) — not indicated in acute hepatitis without cirrhosis/portal HTN.
Intubation is invasive. Aspiration pneumonia alone does not mandate intubation — try oxygen first. Only intubate if P/F ratio <200 or failed NIPPV.
Hepatitis A is fecal-oral. Contact precautions. Post-exposure prophylaxis for family (vaccine or immunoglobulin).
Meperidine is contraindicated in hepatic impairment — normeperidine accumulation → neurotoxicity, seizures.
Always check INR in liver disease — synthetic function is more important than transaminase levels for prognosis.
Transfer to inpatient/ICU for acute hepatitis with LFTs >2000 — need to monitor downward trajectory.
COC — island stop: intractable vomiting in a returning traveler = Hepatitis A until proven otherwise, not motion sickness. The island clinic treated a symptom and missed the disease.
COC — flight home: jaundice appeared at altitude. Lower cabin pressure + hypoxemia = bilirubin more visible in the skin. Hepatocellular injury peaked during the cruise.
COC — car ride: vomit flooding the car during ED transport. The aspiration pneumonia was acquired en route to the hospital, not on the cruise. RLL infiltrate = aspiration in the car.
